claim: Electrical coupling, mediated by gap junctions, contributes to signal averaging, synchronization, and noise reduction in neuronal circuits.
source: Electrical coupling, mediated by gap junctions, contributes to signal averaging, synchronization, and noise reduction in neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is a general statement about gap junction function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Gap junctions may provide alternative neuronal pathways.
source: In addition, gap junctions may also provide alternative neuronal pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential gap junction function.

claim: Gap junctions are small and especially difficult to image.
source: However, because they are small and especially difficult to image, gap junctions are often ignored in large-scale 3D reconstructions.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the technical challenges of imaging gap junctions.

claim: An exuberant spray of fine telodendria extends from each cone pedicle to contact 40–50 nearby rod spherules.
source: An exuberant spray of fine telodendria extends from each cone pedicle (including blue cones) to contact 40–50 nearby rod spherules at sites of Cx36 labeling, with approximately 50 Cx36 clusters per cone pedicle and 2–3 per rod spherule.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript's reconstructions and confocal microscopy.

claim: Blue cone pedicles extend telodendria to contact nearby rod spherules.
source: An exuberant spray of fine telodendria extends from each cone pedicle (including blue cones) to contact 40–50 nearby rod spherules at sites of Cx36 labeling
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing blue cones have similar telodendrial contacts as green cones.

claim: There are approximately 50 Cx36 clusters per cone pedicle.
source: with approximately 50 Cx36 clusters per cone pedicle and 2–3 per rod spherule.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative confocal microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are 2–3 Cx36 clusters per rod spherule.
source: with approximately 50 Cx36 clusters per cone pedicle and 2–3 per rod spherule.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative confocal microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rod/rod coupling was not detected in this study.
source: We were unable to detect rod/rod or cone/cone coupling.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of observed rod/rod gap junctions in the experimental data.

claim: Cone/cone coupling was not detected in this study.
source: We were unable to detect rod/rod or cone/cone coupling.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of observed cone/cone gap junctions in the experimental data.

claim: Rod/cone coupling accounts for nearly all gap junctions between photoreceptors.
source: Thus, rod/cone coupling accounts for nearly all gap junctions between photoreceptors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing abundant rod/cone gap junctions and absence of rod/rod or cone/cone gap junctions.

claim: The mean number of Cx36 channels per rod/cone pair is estimated to be 86.
source: We estimate a mean of 86 Cx36 channels per rod/cone pair
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on morphological measurements from the manuscript.

claim: The maximum conductance of rod/cone gap junctions may be ~1200 pS if all gap junction channels were open.
source: which may provide a maximum conductance of ~1200 pS, if all gap junction channels were open.
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on the number of channels and unitary conductance.

claim: The maximum conductance estimate is comparable to the maximum conductance previously measured between rod/cone pairs in the presence of a dopamine antagonist.
source: This is comparable to the maximum conductance previously measured between rod/cone pairs in the presence of a dopamine antagonist to activate Cx36
evidence: This claim compares the morphological estimate with previously published physiological measurements.

claim: The open probability of gap junction channels can approach 100% under certain conditions.
source: suggesting that the open probability of gap junction channels can approach 100% under certain conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between morphological estimates and physiological measurements.

claim: Gap junctions contain clusters of intercellular channels that allow the passage of ions and other small molecules.
source: Gap junctions contain clusters of intercellular channels that allow the passage of ions and other small molecules, and so support electrical coupling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junction structure and function.

claim: At a gap junction, the membranes of two neighboring cells are closely apposed, leaving only a 2–4 nm gap.
source: At a gap junction, the membranes of two neighboring cells are closely apposed or 'zippered,' leaving only a 2–4 nm gap (Bloomfield and Völgyi, 2009; Miller and Pereda, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junction structure supported by citations.

claim: Each gap junction channel is formed of two docked hemichannels, or connexons.
source: Each gap junction channel is formed of two docked hemichannels, or connexons, and each connexon is assembled from six connexin subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junction molecular structure.

claim: Each connexon is assembled from six connexin subunits.
source: Each gap junction channel is formed of two docked hemichannels, or connexons, and each connexon is assembled from six connexin subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about connexon molecular structure.

claim: Connexin expression is required on both sides to form a gap junction.
source: Connexin expression is required on both sides to form a gap junction (Miller et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The vertebrate connexin family in mouse includes 20 members.
source: The vertebrate connexin family in mouse includes 20 members, including Cx36, the most common neuronal connexin (Beyer and Berthoud, 2009; Söhl et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cx36 is the most common neuronal connexin.
source: The vertebrate connexin family in mouse includes 20 members, including Cx36, the most common neuronal connexin (Beyer and Berthoud, 2009; Söhl et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Homologous gap junctions between cells of the same type support the lateral spread of signals through coupled networks.
source: Homologous gap junctions between cells of the same type support the lateral spread of signals through coupled networks that can average over a wider area than a single neuron, as would be expected for rod/rod or cone/cone coupling, if they were shown to occur.
evidence: This is a general principle about homologous coupling based on established knowledge.

claim: Heterologous coupling between different cell types can provide specific connections to form another neuronal pathway or an alternative route for signal flow.
source: In addition, heterologous coupling between different cell types can provide the specific connections to form another neuronal pathway or an alternative route for signal flow.
evidence: This is a general principle about heterologous coupling based on established knowledge.

claim: Rod/cone coupling provides an alternative pathway for rod signals to enter cone-driven circuits, known as the secondary rod pathway.
source: For example, rod/cone coupling provides an alternative pathway for rod signals to enter cone-driven circuits, known as the secondary rod pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the secondary rod pathway.

claim: Gap junction connections between AII amacrine cells and ON bipolar cells support the primary rod pathway.
source: The gap junction connections between AII amacrine cells and ON bipolar cells in the retina, which support the primary rod pathway, are another well-known example of heterologous coupling (Demb and Singer, 2012; Feigenspan et al., 2001; Mills et al., 2001; Veruki and Hartveit, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gap junctions play roles in signal averaging, noise reduction, synchronization, and predictive coding.
source: While the distribution of gap junctions is widespread in neural tissue and their roles in signal averaging, noise reduction, synchronization, and predictive coding have been well documented (Connors, 2017; Nagy et al., 2018)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gap junctions are small, difficult to image, and often ignored.
source: they are small, difficult to image, and often ignored.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges of studying gap junctions based on established knowledge.

claim: The role of electrical coupling in neural circuits may be underappreciated and poorly understood.
source: Thus, the role of electrical coupling in neural circuits may be underappreciated and poorly understood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difficulty of studying gap junctions.

claim: It is challenging to reliably identify gap junctions in electron microscopy material.
source: Indeed, it is challenging to reliably identify gap junctions in electron microscopy (EM) material (Pallotto et al., 2015)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Gap junctions may be absent from large-scale serial EM reconstructions.
source: and gap junctions may be absent from large-scale serial EM reconstructions (Kasthuri et al., 2015; Scheffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: This study demonstrates an approach for measuring small gap junctions reliably in the mouse retina that can be applied to other parts of the brain.
source: In this study, we demonstrate an approach for measuring small gap junctions reliably in the mouse retina that can be applied to other parts of the brain.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Cone pedicles are found in a single layer in the mid-OPL.
source: Cone pedicles are found in a single layer in the mid-OPL, whereas the smaller rod spherules are found above and between the cone pedicles in the top (distal) half of the OPL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal anatomy.

claim: Rod spherules are found above and between the cone pedicles in the top (distal) half of the OPL.
source: Cone pedicles are found in a single layer in the mid-OPL, whereas the smaller rod spherules are found above and between the cone pedicles in the top (distal) half of the OPL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal anatomy.

claim: In the mouse retina, rods outnumber cones by about 30-1.
source: In the mouse retina, rods outnumber cones by about 30-1 (Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The OPL is numerically dominated by rod spherules.
source: and, numerically, the OPL is dominated by rod spherules.
evidence: This is inferred from the rod to cone ratio.

claim: Cone pedicles are the largest structures in the OPL.
source: Cone pedicles are the largest structures in the OPL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal anatomy.

claim: Cone pedicles contain numerous synaptic ribbons, each marking an active zone.
source: They contain numerous synaptic ribbons, each marking an active zone, and make synaptic contacts with horizontal cells and 13 types of cone bipolar cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cone pedicle structure.

claim: Cone pedicles make synaptic contacts with horizontal cells and 13 types of cone bipolar cell.
source: They contain numerous synaptic ribbons, each marking an active zone, and make synaptic contacts with horizontal cells and 13 types of cone bipolar cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cone pedicle connectivity.

claim: CBC9 bipolar cells contact short wavelength-sensitive (blue) cones selectively.
source: One of these bipolar cell types, CBC9, contacts short wavelength-sensitive (i.e., 'blue') cones selectively, which can be identified on this basis (Behrens et al., 2016; Nadal-Nicolás et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Blue cones can be identified by their selective contacts with CBC9 bipolar cells.
source: One of these bipolar cell types, CBC9, contacts short wavelength-sensitive (i.e., 'blue') cones selectively, which can be identified on this basis (Behrens et al., 2016; Nadal-Nicolás et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations used as a method in this study.

claim: Rod spherules contain a single large ribbon.
source: Rod spherules contain a single large ribbon and synapse with horizontal cells and a single type of rod bipolar cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rod spherule structure.

claim: Rod spherules synapse with horizontal cells and a single type of rod bipolar cell.
source: Rod spherules contain a single large ribbon and synapse with horizontal cells and a single type of rod bipolar cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rod spherule connectivity.

claim: Numerous, small gap junctions in the OPL were first described in early ultrastructural studies in cat and primate retinas.
source: The numerous, small gap junctions in the OPL were first described in early ultrastructural studies in cat and primate retinas (Kolb, 1977; Raviola and Gilula, 1973; Smith et al., 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Basal processes called telodendria spread laterally from cone pedicles to make small gap junctions with rod spherules.
source: Basal processes, called telodendria, spread laterally from cone pedicles to make small gap junctions with rod spherules.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: In freeze-fracture EM, the gap junctions appear as strings of single particles curved around the synaptic invagination of rod spherules.
source: In freeze-fracture EM, the gap junctions appear as strings of single particles curved around the synaptic invagination of rod spherules (Raviola and Gilula, 1973).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The presence of gap junctions at rod/cone contacts is consistent with the electrical transmission of rod signals to cones, forming the secondary rod pathway.
source: The presence of gap junctions at rod/cone contacts is consistent with the electrical transmission of rod signals to cones, forming the secondary rod pathway in which rod signals influence cone-driven circuits (Asteriti et al., 2014; Ingram et al., 2019; Li et al., 2010; Nelson, 1977; Ribelayga et al., 2008; Ribelayga and Mangel, 2010; Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rods and cones both express Cx36, but no other connexins.
source: Rods and cones both express Cx36, but no other connexins (Bloomfield and Völgyi, 2009; Jin et al., 2020; O'Brien et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cx36-mediated rod/cone coupling accounts for most of the gap junctions in the OPL.
source: with Cx36-mediated rod/cone coupling accounting for most of the gap junctions in the OPL (Asteriti et al., 2017; Ingram et al., 2019; Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cone/cone coupling has been reported in cat and primate retinae.
source: In addition to rod/cone gap junctions, cone/cone coupling has been reported in cat and primate retinae (Kolb, 1977; Smith et al., 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rod/rod gap junctions have been suggested from tracer coupling studies and EM studies of the mouse retina.
source: Rod/rod gap junctions have been suggested from tracer coupling studies and EM studies of the mouse retina (Jin et al., 2015; Li et al., 2012; Tsukamoto et al., 2001)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In salamander retina, rods are extensively electrically coupled.
source: and, in salamander retina, rods are extensively electrically coupled (Zhang and Wu, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The evidence for rod/rod gap junctions in the mammalian retina is mixed.
source: However, the evidence for rod/rod gap junctions in the mammalian retina is mixed (Bloomfield and Völgyi, 2009; Bolte et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2020; Tsukamoto et al., 2001) and will be addressed here.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: The study used a publicly available SBF-SEM dataset (e2006) which contains photoreceptor terminals and the OPL.
source: We used a publicly available SBF-SEM dataset (e2006; Helmstaedter et al., 2013), which contains photoreceptor terminals and the OPL, to map membrane contacts between photoreceptors.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: The e2006 dataset was prepared to enhance membrane contrast and facilitate tracing neuronal processes, making gap junctions not identifiable.
source: Unfortunately, because this dataset was prepared to enhance membrane contrast and facilitate tracing neuronal processes, gap junctions were not identifiable.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the e2006 dataset.

claim: Confocal microscopy was used to identify the location of Cx36 gap junctions on rod spherules.
source: To work around this problem, we used confocal microscopy to identify the location of Cx36 gap junctions on rod spherules (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study.

claim: Tracing the contacts between cone telodendria and rod spherules in the SBF-SEM dataset revealed numerous potential sites that corresponded with the location of Cx36 immunofluorescence in the confocal dataset.
source: Tracing the contacts between cone telodendria and rod spherules in the SBF-SEM dataset revealed numerous potential sites that corresponded with the location of Cx36 immunofluorescence in the confocal dataset.
evidence: This describes a finding from combining SBF-SEM and confocal data.

claim: The combination of confocal microscopy and SBF-SEM is complementary.
source: Thus, the combination of confocal microscopy and SBF-SEM is complementary.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological approach.

claim: FIB-SEM on new samples processed to preserve ultrastructure was used to confirm the location of rod/cone gap junctions.
source: To confirm the location of rod/cone gap junctions, we used FIB-SEM on new samples processed to preserve ultrastructure, which allowed high-resolution imaging of contacts between cone pedicles and rod spherules.
evidence: This describes a method used in the study.

claim: Heterologous rod/cone gap junctions account for the vast majority of gap junctions in the OPL.
source: We confirmed that heterologous rod/cone gap junctions account for the vast majority of gap junctions in the OPL (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and a citation.

claim: The combination of imaging methods enabled determination of the pattern of connectivity between photoreceptors and a quantitative estimate of rod/cone coupling.
source: The combination of imaging methods enabled us to determine the pattern of connectivity between photoreceptors and make a quantitative estimate of rod/cone coupling, based on gap junction size and number.
evidence: This describes a finding from the study.

claim: Morphological data was correlated with previously published measurements of gap junction conductance between photoreceptors obtained from paired rod/cone recordings.
source: Finally, we correlated this morphological data with our previously published measurements of gap junction conductance between photoreceptors obtained from paired rod/cone recordings (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes an analysis combining morphological and physiological data.

claim: Most connexon channels, up to 100% under certain conditions, can contribute to the wide dynamic range of rod/cone gap junctions.
source: Our calculations suggest that most connexon channels, up to 100% under certain conditions, can contribute to the wide dynamic range of these small, string-like gap junctions between rods and cones.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on calculations combining morphological and physiological data.

claim: Immunofluorescent labeling for Cx36 revealed small clusters of labeling in the OPL.
source: Immunofluorescent labeling for Cx36 revealed small clusters of labeling in the OPL (Figure 1A, red).
evidence: This is a direct observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An antibody to the vesicular glutamate transporter (vGlut1) was used to identify rod spherules.
source: To locate these potential gap junctions, we used an antibody to the vesicular glutamate transporter (vGlut1) (Figure 1B, blue) to identify rod spherules
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figure 1B.

claim: An antibody to cone arrestin (CAR) was used to label cone pedicles.
source: and an antibody to cone arrestin (CAR) to label cone pedicles (Figure 1C, green).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Labeling with the CAR antibody stains cones in their entirety from the outer segment to the pedicle.
source: Labeling with the CAR antibody stains cones in their entirety from the outer segment to the pedicle (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: Fine processes called telodendria extend laterally from each cone pedicle to form an overlapping matrix in the OPL.
source: Fine processes, called telodendria (e.g., oblique arrows in Figure 1C), extend laterally from each cone pedicle to form an overlapping matrix in the OPL.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The area between and above the cone pedicles is filled with numerous vGlut1-labeled rod spherules.
source: The area between and above the cone pedicles is filled with numerous vGlut1-labeled rod spherules while the space underneath is occupied by the dendrites of horizontal cells and bipolar cells.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: The space underneath cone pedicles is occupied by the dendrites of horizontal cells and bipolar cells.
source: The area between and above the cone pedicles is filled with numerous vGlut1-labeled rod spherules while the space underneath is occupied by the dendrites of horizontal cells and bipolar cells.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: Cone telodendria rose above the level of the cone pedicles to contact the overlying rod spherules.
source: The cone telodendria rose above the level of the cone pedicles to contact the overlying rod spherules (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the OPL, there are many small Cx36 clusters associated with cone telodendria, often at their tips, relatively high (distal) in the OPL.
source: In the OPL, there are many small Cx36 clusters associated with cone telodendria, often at their tips, relatively high (distal) in the OPL.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: Cx36 clusters are contained within the band of vGlut1-labeled rod spherules.
source: Staining the rod spherules for a synaptic vesicle marker, such as the vesicular glutamate transporter, shows that Cx36 clusters are contained within the band of vGlut1-labeled rod spherules (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was almost no Cx36 labeling in the outer nuclear layer (ONL).
source: There was almost no Cx36 labeling in the outer nuclear layer (ONL).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: The absence of Cx36 labeling in the ONL rules out the presence of Cx36 gap junctions between rod somas and/or passing axons in the ONL.
source: This is important because it rules out the presence of Cx36 gap junctions between rod somas and/or passing axons in the ONL, where they are packed together at high density.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of no Cx36 labeling in the ONL.

claim: Cx36 clusters are apparent distinctly underneath each cone pedicle on processes previously identified as bipolar cell dendrites.
source: Cx36 clusters are also apparent distinctly underneath each cone pedicle (vertical arrowheads, Figure 1), on processes previously identified as bipolar cell dendrites (Feigenspan et al., 2004; O'Brien et al., 2012; Raviola and Gilula, 1973).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1, supported by citations.

claim: Cx36 clusters underneath cone pedicles are excluded from analysis because they are not colocalized with cone pedicles.
source: Because they are not colocalized with cone pedicles, they are excluded from further analysis in this article.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the study.

claim: A transgenic mouse line, Opn4cre;Z/EG, was used where there is sparse labeling of a few individual cones.
source: Therefore, we turned to a transgenic mouse line, Opn4cre;Z/EG (Ecker et al., 2010), where there is sparse labeling of a few individual cones (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Individual EGFP-labeled cones were viewed against a background of all cones stained for CAR.
source: This made it possible to view individual EGFP-labeled cones against a background of all cones stained for CAR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence data were analyzed by extracting only the Cx36 clusters that colocalized with EGFP-labeled pedicles.
source: The immunofluorescence data were analyzed by extracting only the Cx36 clusters that colocalized with EGFP-labeled pedicles (Figure 2C) and reconstructing in 3D to find the number and location of Cx36 clusters on a single-cone pedicle (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: At each Cx36 cluster, there is an adjacent rod spherule.
source: At each Cx36 cluster, there is an adjacent rod spherule (Figure 2E), suggesting that these structures are rod/cone gap junctions.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There are approximately 51.4 ± 8.88 (mean ± SD, n = 18, three retinae) Cx36 clusters on each cone pedicle.
source: There are approximately 51.4 ± 8.88 (mean ± SD, n = 18, three retinae) Cx36 clusters on each cone pedicle (Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—source data 1), along the telodendria and over the upper surface of the cone pedicle.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from confocal microscopy shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claim: Cx36 clusters are located along the telodendria and over the upper surface of the cone pedicle.
source: There are approximately 51.4 ± 8.88 (mean ± SD, n = 18, three retinae) Cx36 clusters on each cone pedicle (Figure 2D and F, Figure 2—source data 1), along the telodendria and over the upper surface of the cone pedicle.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claim: Blue cones in the dorsal retina were stained in their entirety by use of a blue cone opsin Venus transgenic mouse line.
source: Blue cones in the dorsal retina were stained in their entirety by use of a blue cone opsin Venus transgenic mouse line (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Blue cones were identified using an antibody to blue cone opsin to stain the outer segment and then following the CAR-labeled axon down to the pedicle in a confocal series.
source: Alternatively, blue cones were identified using an antibody to blue cone opsin to stain the outer segment and then following the CAR-labeled axon down to the pedicle in a confocal series (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A sparse mosaic of 'true blue' cones was located in the dorsal retina.
source: In either case, a sparse mosaic of 'true blue' cones was located in the dorsal retina, as opposed to the ventral retina where most cones express both blue (S) and green (M) opsins (Nadal-Nicolás et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy supported by a citation.

claim: In the ventral retina, most cones express both blue (S) and green (M) opsins.
source: In either case, a sparse mosaic of 'true blue' cones was located in the dorsal retina, as opposed to the ventral retina where most cones express both blue (S) and green (M) opsins (Nadal-Nicolás et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The pedicles of blue cones have telodendria-bearing Cx36-labeled clusters in a manner indistinguishable from green cone pedicles.
source: We find that the pedicles of blue cones have telodendria-bearing Cx36-labeled clusters in a manner indistinguishable from green cone pedicles (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Blue cones make numerous Cx36 gap junctions with rods.
source: Thus, it appears that blue cones also make numerous Cx36 gap junctions with rods.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blue cones have Cx36 clusters similar to green cones.

claim: In high-resolution confocal images, the Cx36 elements occur exclusively where cone telodendria contact the base of each rod spherule.
source: In high-resolution confocal images (×63 objective, NA 1.4, Zeiss Airyscan), the Cx36 elements occur exclusively where cone telodendria contact the base of each rod spherule (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from high-resolution confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Some rod/cone contacts have multiple Cx36 clusters.
source: Some rod/cone contacts have multiple Cx36 clusters (Figure 3A, arrow).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Rod spherules appear as oval structures including two unlabeled compartments or holes, separated by the synaptic ribbon.
source: In these images, rod spherules appear as oval structures (blue) including two unlabeled compartments or holes, separated by the synaptic ribbon, immunolabeled for ribeye (Figure 3B, white).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lower hole in the rod spherule contains the mGluR6-labeled tips of rod bipolar cell dendrites and was identified as the postsynaptic compartment.
source: The lower hole in the rod spherule of Figure 3B contains the mGluR6-labeled (green) tips of rod bipolar cell dendrites and was thus identified as the postsynaptic compartment.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The upper hole in the rod spherule contains a single large mitochondrion, labeled for the mitochondrial translocase TOMM20.
source: The upper hole contains a single large mitochondrion, labeled for the mitochondrial translocase TOMM20 (red).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A mean structure was generated by aligning, stacking, and averaging the images from 18 complete rod spherules from a single section.
source: To quantitatively determine the position of Cx36-labeled points, we captured vGlut1-labeled rod spherules and generated a mean structure by aligning, stacking, and averaging the images from 18 complete rod spherules from a single section.
evidence: This describes a method used in the study.

claim: Cx36 elements were found to be located around the base of the mean rod spherule.
source: The sites of individual Cx36 elements were marked and found to be located around the base of the mean rod spherule (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Cx36 is distributed around the mouth of the synaptic opening, shown by a drop in the vGlut1 labeling.
source: The twin peaks of the resulting curve show that Cx36 (red) is distributed around the mouth of the synaptic opening, shown by a drop in the vGlut1 labeling (blue) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the same region where Cx36 is high, the labeling for the cone signal is high, suggesting that Cx36 gap junctions occur at telodendrial contact points with rods.
source: In the same region, the labeling for the cone signal (green) is high, suggesting that Cx36 gap junctions occur at telodendrial contact points with rods.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In a sample of 18 rod spherules, there were 45 Cx36 clusters, yielding 2.50 ± 0.764 Cx36 clusters/rod (mean ± SD).
source: In this sample of 18 rod spherules, there were 45 Cx36 clusters, yielding 2.50 ± 0.764 Cx36 clusters/rod (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from confocal microscopy.

claim: From the mean structure of 18 rod spherules, all Cx36 elements were located at the base of the rod spherule, within 1–2 μm of the opening to the postsynaptic compartment.
source: From the mean structure of these 18 rod spherules, all Cx36 elements were located at the base of the rod spherule, within 1–2 μm of the opening to the postsynaptic compartment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: From seven different sections, from three retinae, all 260 rod spherules analyzed have cone contacts and Cx36 labeling close to the synaptic opening.
source: From seven different sections, from three retinae, all 260 rod spherules analyzed have cone contacts and Cx36 labeling close to the synaptic opening (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from confocal microscopy supported by a citation.

claim: The number of Cx36 elements per rod spherule ranged from 1 to 6 with a mean of 2.48 ± 1.01 (mean ± SD).
source: Frequently, there are multiple Cx36-labeled points at the base of a single rod spherule; the number of Cx36 elements ranged from 1 to 6 with a mean of 2.48 ± 1.01 (mean ± SD) (Figure 3F and G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from confocal microscopy shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Every rod spherule was coupled to a nearby cone.
source: Presuming that a Cx36 cluster indicates the presence of a gap junction, we conclude that every rod spherule was coupled to a nearby cone.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that all 260 rod spherules had Cx36 labeling.

claim: The e2006 SBF-SEM dataset is derived from a block of mouse retina including 164 cone pedicles and thousands of rod spherules with a voxel size of 16.5 × 16.5 × 25 nm.

claim: Cone pedicles are easily recognized as the largest structures in the OPL in the e2006 dataset.

claim: Rod spherules were easily identified as the numerous round and compact structures with prominent postsynaptic inclusions in the synaptic invagination.

claim: Rod spherules are massed above and surrounding the cone pedicles, usually oriented with the synaptic invagination at the base.
source: In this dataset, rod spherules are 2–3 μm in diameter and they are massed above and surrounding the cone pedicles (Figure 4B), usually oriented with the synaptic invagination at the base.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A patch of 29 adjacent cones was chosen to skeletonize.

claim: The patch of 29 cones included 13 central cone pedicles within a ring surrounded by an annulus of 16 additional cone pedicles.

claim: Some calculations were based on the central 13 cones to avoid edge artifacts.
source: Some calculations were based on the central 13 cones to avoid edge artifacts.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the study.

claim: The central area contained one blue cone pedicle.
source: This central area contained one blue cone pedicle, but, in addition, we analyzed all the blue cone pedicles in the dataset (Figure 4A), as identified by Behrens et al., 2016 (summarized in Appendix 2—table 2).

claim: All the blue cone pedicles in the dataset were analyzed.

claim: Several other locations, including an area with a sparse distribution of cone pedicles, were examined to ensure the selected area was not atypical.

claim: The mosaic of cone pedicles with their overlapping telodendria is plotted in Figure 4C.

claim: The telodendria are contained within the upper part of the OPL.
source: Cone axons were followed into the ONL, and a projection shows that the telodendria are contained within the upper part of the OPL (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cone 5 has a complex but typical field of telodendria approximately 10 µm in diameter.
source: We started our analysis with a single-cone pedicle (cone 5), near the center, which had a complex but typical field of telodendria approximately 10 µm in diameter, and we marked the position of every rod spherule in contact with this cone (Figure 5A).

claim: Cone 5 has contacts with 34 rod spherules that included every rod spherule within the telodendrial field.
source: Cone 5 has contacts with 34 rod spherules that included every rod spherule within the telodendrial field.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: The telodendria extend laterally and above the cone pedicle, reaching up to the overlying rod spherules.
source: In a projection, it can be seen that the telodendria extend laterally and above the cone pedicle, reaching up to the overlying rod spherules (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many, but not all, telodendria terminate at the base of a rod spherule.
source: Many, but not all, telodendria terminate at the base of a rod spherule.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: The skeleton of a blue cone pedicle (cone 2) is similar to green cone pedicles.
source: The skeleton of a blue cone pedicle (cone 2) is similar (Figure 5A, bottom, B and C, arrow).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: Each cone contacts 43.0 ± 5.40 rod spherules (mean ± SD, n = 29 cones).
source: Each cone contacts 43.0 ± 5.40 rod spherules (mean ± SD, n = 29 cones) (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 1), including every rod spherule within its field, typically at the base.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Each cone contacts every rod spherule within its field, typically at the base.
source: Each cone contacts 43.0 ± 5.40 rod spherules (mean ± SD, n = 29 cones) (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 1), including every rod spherule within its field, typically at the base.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There is a slight trend for the largest cone pedicles to contact more rod spherules.
source: Plotting convergence (number of rod spherule contacts per cone) against the pedicle area shows a slight trend for the largest cone pedicles to contact more rods spherules (Figure 5H, Figure 5—source data 1).

claim: Most rods are contacted by two or three cone pedicles.
source: Examining these contacts from the perspective of the rod spherules, we coded the overlying rod spherules in the same color as each cone pedicle. Rod spherules with contacts from two or three of the central 13 cone pedicles are marked black or dark gray, respectively, with noncontacted rod spherules marked as light gray. Viewing the resulting map quickly makes the point that most rods are contacted by two or three cone pedicles (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 3/811 (0.4%) rods were found without cone contacts within the field of 29 cones.
source: We found 3/811 (0.4%) rods without cone contacts within the field of 29 cones, an insignificant fraction.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: In a sparse patch with a rare hole in the cone mosaic, more than 95% of rods received cone contacts.
source: As a precaution, we also checked a sparse patch with a rare hole in the cone mosaic (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D). Even here, more than 95% of rods received cone contacts.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Of approximately 40 rods in contact with each cone pedicle, only a few have exclusive contacts with a single cone (7.23 ± 3.38, mean ± SD, n = 13 central cone pedicles).
source: Of approximately 40 rods in contact with each cone pedicle, only a few have exclusive contacts with a single cone (7.23 ± 3.38, mean ± SD, n = 13 central cone pedicles).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: Adjacent cone pedicles share as many as 23 rod spherules, (mean ± SD = 6.23 ± 4.67, n = 79 cone pairs).
source: Most rods receive contacts from several cone pedicles while adjacent cone pedicles share as many as 23 rod spherules, (mean ± SD = 6.23 ± 4.67, n = 79 cone pairs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 74% of rod spherules received contacts from two or three cones, yielding a rod to cone divergence of 1.89.
source: In this area, rods with multiple cone contacts were the norm; 74% of rod spherules received contacts from two or three cones, yielding a rod to cone divergence of 1.89 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Each rod spherule has the potential to make several contacts with close-by cones.
source: Clearly, each rod spherule has the potential to make several contacts with close-by cones, in agreement with the confocal data showing the distribution of Cx36.
evidence: This is an inference from the SBF-SEM data consistent with confocal data.

claim: The telodendrial area of blue cones was 85.1 ± 18.6 μm2 (mean ± SD, n = 5).
source: The telodendrial area of blue cones was 85.1 ± 18.6 μm2 (mean ± SD, n = 5) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Blue cones contact all rod spherules within their telodendrial field (convergence 39.8 ± 5.11, mean ± SD, n = 5).
source: Like green cones, blue cones contact all rod spherules, within their telodendrial field (convergence 39.8 ± 5.11, mean ± SD, n = 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: The convergence in blue cones fell within the range of rods in contact with green cones, 43.0 ± 5.40 rod spherules (mean ± SD, n = 29).
source: The convergence in blue cones fell within the range of rods in contact with green cones, 43.0 ± 5.40 rod spherules (mean ± SD, n = 29).
evidence: This is a comparison of quantitative findings from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: Most of the rods in contact with a blue cone also receive contact from adjacent overlapping green cones.
source: Most of the rods in contact with a blue cone also receive contact from adjacent overlapping green cones.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: There is no evidence for color-selective rod contacts.
source: Thus, there is no evidence for color-selective rod contacts.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that blue and green cones contact the same rods.

claim: Several cone pedicles and the rod spherules contacted by each cone pedicle were segmented.
source: We segmented several cone pedicles and the rod spherules contacted by each cone pedicle.
evidence: This describes a method used in the study.

claim: The contact sites, where the cell membrane of a cone telodendron combined with the cell membrane of a rod spherule, with no visible space between them, were highlighted.
source: The contact sites, where the cell membrane of a cone telodendron combined with the cell membrane of a rod spherule, with no visible space between them, were highlighted (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This describes a method used in the study shown in Figures 6A–D.

claim: The telodendrial contacts, often from more than one cone, appear as arcs, close to the synaptic opening of rod spherules.
source: Typically, the telodendrial contacts, often from more than one cone, appear as arcs, close to the synaptic opening of rod spherules (Kolb, 1977; Smith et al., 1986; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset supported by citations.

claim: Confocal analysis demonstrated multiple cone contacts with a single rod spherule.
source: Confocal analysis also demonstrated multiple cone contacts with a single rod spherule (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Some rod spherules sit directly astride a cone pedicle and receive few or no telodendrial contacts, instead making direct contacts with the roof of the cone pedicle.
source: There are a few anomalies in the OPL: some rod spherules sit directly astride a cone pedicle and receive few or no telodendrial contacts. Instead, they make direct contacts with the roof of the cone pedicle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lowest (most proximal) row of rods in the ONL do not have axons or spherules; instead, the synaptic machinery is included in the lowest crescent of the cell body, adjacent to the OPL.
source: In addition, the lowest (most proximal) row of rods in the ONL do not have axons or spherules (Li et al., 2016). Instead, the synaptic machinery is included in the lowest crescent of the cell body, adjacent to the OPL.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset supported by a citation.

claim: Low rods in the ONL still receive contacts from cone telodendria.
source: These low rods represent the most distal synaptic structures in the OPL, yet they still receive contacts from cone telodendria (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are a few rod spherules below (proximal to) the level of the cone pedicles that are often inverted so the mouth is on top, and this is the site of telodendrial contacts.
source: Finally, there are a few rod spherules below (proximal to) the level of the cone pedicles. These are often inverted so the mouth is on top, and this is the site of telodendrial contacts (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In every case, including anatomical variations, cone contacts occur close to the rod synaptic opening, coincident with the location of Cx36.
source: Thus, in every case, including these anatomical variations, cone contacts occur close to the rod synaptic opening, coincident with the location of Cx36.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the SBF-SEM and confocal data.

claim: These sites very probably contain Cx36 rod/cone gap junctions.
source: These sites very probably contain Cx36 rod/cone gap junctions.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation of contact sites with Cx36 location.

claim: The telodendrial field of cone 2, a blue cone, contacts 41 rod spherules and overlaps substantially with the surrounding cones.
source: The telodendrial field of cone 2, a blue cone, contacts 41 rod spherules and overlaps substantially with the surrounding cones (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The blue cone pedicle made the same types of rod contacts as other cones, including telodendrial contacts, roof contacts, and contacts with the rods in the bottom row of the ONL.
source: This blue cone pedicle made the same types of rod contacts as other cones, including telodendrial contacts, roof contacts, and contacts with the rods in the bottom row of the ONL (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Blue cone pedicles make typical contact pads around the mouth of the overlying rod spherules with alternating contributions from multiple cones.
source: Reconstructing in 3D shows typical contact pads around the mouth of the overlying rod spherules with alternating contributions from multiple cones, including this blue cone (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Blue cone pedicles make rod/cone gap junctions.
source: Thus, blue cone pedicles also make rod/cone gap junctions and both blue and green cones can make gap junctions with the same rod.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that blue cones have similar contacts as green cones.

claim: Both blue and green cones can make gap junctions with the same rod.
source: Thus, blue cone pedicles also make rod/cone gap junctions and both blue and green cones can make gap junctions with the same rod.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: No evidence of color-specific coupling was found.
source: We found no evidence of color-specific coupling.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the SBF-SEM data.

claim: In an SBF-SEM dataset (eel001), a roof contact between a cone pedicle and an overlying rod spherule shows a darkly stained chromophilic area where the membranes merge, indicating a gap junction approximately 350 nm in length.
source: In Figure 7A and B, a roof contact between a cone pedicle and an overlying rod spherule is shown. There is clear separation between the cell membranes until a darkly stained chromophilic area where the membranes merge, indicating a gap junction approximately 350 nm in length.
evidence: This is an observation from the SBF-SEM dataset (eel001) shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: In a brief survey of the SBF-SEM data, 13 examples of darkly stained merged membranes at rod/cone contacts were found.
source: In a brief survey of the SBF-SEM data, we found 13 examples of darkly stained merged membranes at rod/cone contacts, and a much larger number in the FIB-SEM dataset (see below).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SBF-SEM dataset.

claim: Cx36 occurs at contacts between rods and cones, confirming the presence of a gap junction.
source: We have shown above that Cx36 occurs at such contacts between rods and cones and therefore conclude that this confirms the presence of a gap junction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation of Cx36 labeling with contact sites.

claim: Two FIB-SEM datasets of mouse OPL (FIB-SEM 1 and FIB-SEM 2) with 4 nm voxels were obtained.
source: Thus, we also obtained two FIB-SEM datasets of mouse OPL (FIB-SEM 1 and FIB-SEM 2) with 4 nm voxels revealing electron-dense staining consistent with the size and position of Cx36 labeling, which we interpret as gap junctions.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition for the study.

claim: Contacts from cone telodendria at the base of each rod spherule show darkly stained gap junctions in the same position as Cx36 labeling determined by confocal microscopy.
source: Contacts from cone telodendria at the base of each rod spherule show darkly stained gap junctions (Figure 7C and D) in the same position as Cx36 labeling determined by confocal microscopy (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM dataset shown in Figures 7C and 7D, correlated with confocal data in Figure 3.

claim: The area of telodendrial contact is frequently larger than the size of the gap junction.
source: It should be noted that the area of telodendrial contact is frequently larger than the size of the gap junction (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM dataset shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Contact pads in the SBF-SEM e2006 images indicate the potential for a gap junction but do not predict its size.
source: Thus, while contact pads in the SBF-SEM e2006 images indicate the potential for a gap junction (Figure 6H–K), they do not predict its size.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing SBF-SEM and FIB-SEM data shown in Figures 6H–K.

claim: What appear as small separate gap junctions in a single section can merge in nearby sections to form one large continuous gap junction.
source: Sometimes, what appear as small separate gap junctions in a single section merge in nearby sections to form one large continuous gap junction.
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM dataset.

claim: An example shows two small gap junctions on either side of the synaptic opening that are part of a horseshoe structure.
source: An example is shown in Figure 7E–H; two small gap junctions on either side of the synaptic opening are part of a horseshoe structure similar in shape to many of the reconstructed contact pads.
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM dataset shown in Figures 7E–H.

claim: Reconstructing in 3D shows one large gap junction encircling the base of the rod spherule with a length of approximately 1.5 µm.
source: Reconstructing in 3D shows one large gap junction encircling the base of the rod spherule with a length of approximately 1.5 µm (Figure 7H, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM dataset shown in Figure 7H.

claim: This curved structure is highly reminiscent of the curved gap junction strings revealed by freeze-fracture EM.
source: This curved structure is highly reminiscent of the curved gap junction strings revealed by freeze-fracture EM (Raviola and Gilula, 1973).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous freeze-fracture EM studies supported by a citation.

claim: A few large gap junctions of a similar shape, >1 µm long, were readily apparent in the confocal view of wholemount retina labeled for Cx36.
source: In the OPL, a few large gap junctions of a similar shape, >1 µm long, were readily apparent in the confocal view of wholemount retina labeled for Cx36 (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy supported by a citation.

claim: 42 complete rod spherules with a total of 135 rod/cone gap junctions were analyzed from the FIB-SEM datasets.
source: We analyzed 42 complete rod spherules with a total of 135 rod/cone gap junctions.
evidence: This describes the scope of the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: In the two FIB-SEM datasets, all 42 rod spherules analyzed have gap junctions close to the mouth of the synaptic compartment consistent with the location of Cx36.
source: In the two FIB-SEM datasets, all 42 rod spherules analyzed have gap junctions close to the mouth of the synaptic compartment consistent with the location of Cx36 (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the FIB-SEM analysis consistent with confocal data shown in Figures 3A–E.

claim: In 112 cases where the contact could be traced back, 100% of the gap junction contacts were identified as a cone.
source: We could not always trace the contact back due to the small volume of these high-resolution datasets, but when it was possible, in 112 cases, 100% of the gap junction contacts were identified as a cone.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: The number of gap junctions per rod spherule ranged from 1 to 6 with a mean of 3.21 ± 1.23 (mean ± SD, n = 135).
source: The number of gap junctions per rod spherule ranged from 1 to 6 with a mean of 3.21 ± 1.23 (mean ± SD, n = 135, Figure 8A, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The mean distance from the center of synaptic mouth was 0.686 ± 0.635 µm, (mean ± SD, n = 135), but this is a skewed distribution.
source: The mean distance from the center of synaptic mouth was 0.686 ± 0.635 µm, (mean ± SD, n = 135), but this is a skewed distribution.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: 84% of gap junctions lay within 1 µm of the synaptic mouth with a median distance of 0.435 µm; 94% were within 2 µm.
source: 84% of gap junctions lay within 1 µm of the synaptic mouth with a median distance of 0.435 µm; 94% were within 2 µm (Figure 8B and C, Figure 8—source data 1), coincident with the position of cone contacts and the location of Cx36 labeling (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figures 8B and 8C, consistent with confocal data in Figures 3C–E.

claim: There were eight gap junctions, 6% of the total, which fell outside the 2 µm range from the synaptic mouth.
source: There were eight gap junctions, 6% of the total, which fell outside this range.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: When outlying gap junctions were traced back, the contacts were identified as cones in every case.
source: When these outliers were traced back, the contacts were identified as cones in every case, so despite their distant location relative to the rod synaptic mouth, they were identified as rod/cone gap junctions.
evidence: This is a finding from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: Rod/cone gap junctions had a relatively uniform width (~120 nm), suggesting a standardized component with a variable length such as a string.
source: En face, the rod/cone gap junctions had a relatively uniform width (~120 nm), suggesting a standardized component with a variable length such as a string, as previously reported in freeze-fracture studies of the OPL (Raviola and Gilula, 1973).
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM analysis consistent with previous freeze-fracture studies supported by a citation.

claim: The uniform width of rod/cone gap junctions is consistent with the low fluorescent intensity of Cx36 in the OPL compared to the IPL, where gap junctions occur predominantly as bright Cx36 clusters representing dense two-dimensional arrays of connexons.
source: This is also consistent with the low fluorescent intensity of Cx36 in the OPL compared to the IPL, where gap junctions occur predominantly in the form of bright Cx36 clusters representing dense two-dimensional arrays of connexons (Kamasawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference from the FIB-SEM data consistent with confocal observations and previous studies supported by a citation.

claim: The mean length of a rod/cone gap junction was 477 ± 227 nm (mean ± SD, n = 135, 42 rods).
source: The mean length of a rod/cone gap junction was 477 ± 227 nm (mean ± SD, n = 135, 42 rods, Figure 8D, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Raviola and Gilula, 1973 reported the photoreceptor gap junctions as strings of single particles with a spacing of 10 nm.
source: Raviola and Gilula, 1973 reported the photoreceptor gap junctions as strings of single particles with a spacing of 10 nm.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: The average rod/cone gap junction contains a string of 48 connexons (477/10 ≅ 48).
source: Therefore, we estimate that the average rod/cone gap junction contains a string of 48 connexons (477/10 ≅ 48).
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on the mean gap junction length and connexon spacing.

claim: The total gap junction length per rod spherule was 1.53 µm ± 0.439 µm (mean ± SD, n = 42) or 150 channels.
source: The total gap junction length per rod spherule was 1.53 µm ± 0.439 µm (mean ± SD, n = 42, Figure 8E, Figure 8—source data 1) or 150 channels.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The largest individual gap junctions occurred when there was only one gap junction per rod spherule.
source: The largest individual gap junctions occurred when there was only one gap junction per rod spherule (Figure 8D, F, and G, red points, Figure 8—source data 1); these were outliers with a length close to the mean total length and they were visible in confocal images as large curved Cx36-labeled structures (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figures 8D, F, and G, consistent with confocal observations supported by a citation.

claim: The quantitative analysis of rod/cone gap junctions from the FIB-SEM data confirms the presence of gap junctions at the sites identified from the contact analysis of SBF-EM dataset e2006 and the confocal analysis of Cx36 labeling.
source: In summary, the quantitative analysis of rod/cone gap junctions from the FIB-SEM data confirms the presence of gap junctions at the sites identified from the contact analysis of SBF-EM dataset e2006 and the confocal analysis of Cx36 labeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined analysis of FIB-SEM, SBF-SEM, and confocal data.

claim: Rod/cone gap junctions appear as concentric strings around the postsynaptic opening, as reported in the original freeze-fracture data.
source: Furthermore, rod/cone gap junctions appear as concentric strings around the postsynaptic opening, as reported in the original freeze-fracture data (Raviola and Gilula, 1973; Reale et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the FIB-SEM data consistent with previous freeze-fracture studies supported by citations.

claim: Six cone pedicles from dataset FIB-SEM 1 were segmented and partially reconstructed to evaluate cone/cone coupling.
source: To evaluate cone/cone coupling, we segmented and partially reconstructed six cone pedicles from dataset FIB-SEM 1.
evidence: This describes a method used in the study.

claim: 22 contacts between six pairs of cones were found, 3–4 contacts per pair.
source: The small size/high resolution of the dataset meant that no cone pedicles were complete. Nevertheless, we found 22 contacts between six pairs of cones, 3–4 contacts per pair (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: A single-cone pedicle could make around 20 contacts with up to six surrounding pedicles given a telodendrial coverage of 1.5.
source: This suggests that a single-cone pedicle could make around 20 contacts with up to six surrounding pedicles given a telodendrial coverage of 1.5.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed contacts between cone pairs.

claim: Cone/cone contacts did not have the typical appearance of a gap junction.
source: Although we were able to locate cone/cone contacts, they did not have the typical appearance of a gap junction.
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: Cone/cone contacts were direct, without intervening glial processes, but there was no clear membrane density.
source: While the contacts were direct, without intervening glial processes, there was no clear membrane density.
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: When a nearby rod/cone gap junction was contained in the same frame as a cone/cone contact, the rod/cone gap junction was much more densely stained.
source: When a nearby rod/cone gap junction was contained in the same frame, it was much more densely stained (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an observation from the FIB-SEM analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: All 22 cone/cone contacts were examined, but no typical electron-dense gap junctions were identified in this material.
source: We examined all 22 cone/cone contacts, but we were unable to identify any typical electron-dense gap junctions in this material.
evidence: This is a finding from the FIB-SEM analysis.

claim: The absence of cone/cone gap junctions is surprising given previous reports of cone/cone coupling in mammals.
source: This is surprising given previous reports of cone/cone coupling in mammals.
